title: Promoting Candidness Starts With Leader Transparency About Major Decisions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that leaders who want more candor from their teams cannot simply ask for it — they must model it first by making their own decision-making radically transparent. The author explains that sharing rationales, alternative arguments, and even meeting notes around major decisions invites team members to ask questions, and that leaders responding to those questions without defensiveness is what actually normalizes honest exchange. Candor is portrayed as a downstream effect of vulnerability at the top, not a cultural value that can be mandated directly. The essay closes by noting that any decision affecting a team member counts, in their eyes, as a major decision worth this kind of transparency.
points: The essay's core claim is directional: candor flows downward from leader transparency about decisions, not upward from demanding honesty from subordinates.
It specifies a concrete mechanism — sharing rationales, alternative arguments, and meeting notes — rather than leaving 'transparency' abstract.
The piece identifies non-defensive response to questions as the pivot point where transparency actually converts into a culture of candor.
It reframes what counts as a 'major decision' from the leader's perspective to the team member's perspective, broadening the practice's scope.
quotes: Simply asking for more candidness is a smart idea but doesn’t usually create much change.
Candid communication in an organization or team starts at the top.
When transparency surrounding decision-making is followed by inquiry, a new openness emerges.
Leaders who want more transparency must give it to others first. Such honesty in discussions about decisions makes leaders vulnerable in the eyes of the team.
It is this vulnerability that promotes everyday candidness from those below. Leaders can never demand more candidness. Just as with trust and respect, they must earn it.
